sysd-found-003.title: Unicast, broadcast, multicast and anycast: who receives a packet
sysd-found-003.text: How many machines should one message reach? IP has four principal addressing methods, unicast, broadcast, multicast and {{ref:sysd-found-201}}, and they differ in how many receivers a message reaches. Unicast delivers a message to one specific node, because each destination address uniquely identifies a single receiver endpoint. It carries traffic such as {{ref:sysd-found-032}}, FTP and SMTP. Broadcast delivers a message to all nodes in the network. One datagram from one sender is routed to every endpoint tied to the broadcast address, generally across an entire subnet. ARP, DHCP and NTP use it, though a broadcast does not mean every receiver gets the message. Multicast delivers a message to a group of nodes that have expressed interest. Its destination address designates a subset, not necessarily all, of the accessible nodes, and IPTV and video conferences use it. Sending the same data to several unicast addresses means sending it once per recipient. With multicast the sender sends a single datagram to the group address, and the routers copy it to all interested receivers. The fourth method delivers a message to any one node out of a group that share the same destination address, typically the nearest. The routing algorithm picks it by some distance or cost measure, and DNS querying and CDNs use it. Sources differ a little here. One describes it as reaching a single device or a specific group, with the other hosts in the group also expected to receive the message.

sysd-found-004.title: MTU and fragmentation: when a packet is too big
sysd-found-004.text: Across Ethernet, no packet may exceed 1500 bytes. That limit is the maximum transmission unit (MTU), the largest packet a link can carry. IPv4 automatically fragments a datagram into smaller units when it exceeds the link's MTU. IPv6 does not fragment in network elements, so end hosts must avoid exceeding the path MTU, which {{ref:sysd-found-150}} can find. TCP adjusts its segment size to stay smaller than the MTU. UDP and ICMP disregard it and force IP to fragment oversized datagrams. On Ethernet the minimum TCP and IPv4 headers are 20 bytes each, so the maximum segment size is 1500 - (20 + 20), or 1460 bytes. Fragmentation has costs. The whole packet is lost if any fragment is dropped. A tunnel header that pushes packets just over the MTU forces two fragments per packet, so every router forwards twice as many packets. A larger MTU is more efficient, but large packets hold a link longer, add delay and cost more to retransmit after an error.

sysd-found-010.title: TCP congestion control: how a sender finds the right speed
sysd-found-010.text: A TCP sender has to guess how fast the network can go, using only acknowledgments and timers. Congestion control is the set of sender-side mechanisms that keep a connection from sending more than the network can carry. The sender keeps a congestion window limiting unacknowledged data in flight. The receive window protects the receiver, and the sender stays within both. Slow start begins with a window of 1, 2, 4 or 10 MSS, where an MSS is one maximum-size segment. The sender adds 1 MSS per ACK, which doubles the window each round trip. This continues until a loss, the receiver's window or the threshold ssthresh stops it. Then congestion avoidance grows the window by up to 1 MSS per round trip. After a timeout loss the sender saves half the window as ssthresh and restarts slow start. Fast retransmit resends a segment after three duplicate acknowledgments instead of waiting for the timer, and fast recovery then halves the window and skips slow start. Treating loss as congestion misfires on wireless links, where fading and interference cause losses.

sysd-found-148.title: ARP: finding the hardware address for an IP address
sysd-found-148.text: To send a packet to 192.168.0.55 on its own network, host A first has to learn that machine's hardware address, so it asks everyone. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the link-layer address, such as a MAC address, that goes with an internet-layer address, typically an IPv4 address. A broadcasts a request to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF containing the target's IP address. Only B answers, with its MAC address, and A then sends the data packet addressed to that MAC. ARP is a request-response protocol carried directly in link-layer frames. It works only within one subnetwork and is never routed. Nodes cache IP-to-MAC mappings so they need not broadcast every time. ARP cannot authenticate replies, so a spoofer can answer for another system's address to intercept its traffic. In IPv6 networks the Neighbor Discovery Protocol does ARP's job. Sources disagree about where ARP sits. RFC 826 and RFC 1122 place it in the link layer. Other textbooks put it in the OSI data link layer, the {{ref:sysd-found-031}} or an intermediate layer 2.5.

sysd-found-012.title: Head-of-line blocking: waiting behind a lost packet
sysd-found-012.text: One lost packet can freeze everything queued behind it. Head-of-line blocking is the delay that occurs when data that arrived later cannot be used until earlier lost or reordered data has been retransmitted and received. TCP offers a reliable byte stream, so the application cannot access packets after a lost one until the retransmitted copy arrives. If independent messages share one TCP connection, a fully received later message must wait for an earlier one. Browsers mitigate this by opening parallel connections. That repeats the connection establishment cost, and each connection runs congestion control on its own instead of pooling information.

sysd-found-149.title: QUIC: a faster transport built on UDP
sysd-found-149.text: TCP treats any error as blocking. When several streams of {{ref:sysd-found-040}} share one TCP connection, a single lost packet stalls all of them. QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol, normally layered on UDP, that carries several streams over one connection and builds TLS into its handshake. UDP has no loss recovery, so QUIC does the recovery itself. Each stream is flow-controlled separately and lost data is retransmitted at the QUIC level, so an error in one stream does not block the others. The key exchange and the list of supported protocols are part of the initial handshake, which cuts connection setup latency. Every packet carries a connection identifier, so a connection survives an IP address change, such as a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular. Many middleboxes, the devices that sit in a network path, rate-limit or block UDP. So Chromium starts a QUIC and a TCP connection at the same time and falls back to TCP. The IETF standardized QUIC in RFC 9000 in May 2021, using {{ref:sysd-found-188}}. Its first application is described in {{ref:sysd-found-041}}.

sysd-found-022.title: Public and private addresses: who can be reached
sysd-found-022.text: At home, every connected device shares one public address from the outside. It is the address the ISP assigns to the whole network. A public IP address is a globally routable unicast address that may be used for communication between hosts on the global Internet. A private address is reserved for use inside a private network. Private ranges are not routed on the Internet and need no coordination with an address registry. A home router hands them to devices such as computers, tablets and phones. Private networks typically reach the Internet through {{ref:sysd-found-028}}, which lets them conserve public address space.

sysd-found-028.title: NAT: how a private network shares one public address
sysd-found-028.text: IPv4 can identify about 4.3 billion devices, yet one Internet-routable address on a NAT gateway can serve an entire private network. Network address translation (NAT) maps one IP address space into another by rewriting address information in packet headers as they cross a routing device. The common one-to-many form maps many private hosts to one public address. A router rewrites outbound source addresses to its public address and tracks each active connection, so replies reach the right host. For TCP and UDP it rewrites port numbers too. It keeps a table of internal address, original source port and translated port. An incoming packet whose destination port is not in the table is dropped or rejected. Outside hosts cannot initiate a connection to an internal host unless port forwarding publishes the service. NAT also breaks end-to-end connectivity. VoIP and other applications that link users directly need application-level gateways or {{ref:sysd-found-145}}. NAT is not commonly used in IPv6, because the large address space lets every device have a unique, globally routable address.

sysd-found-023.title: Static and dynamic addresses: fixed or lent
sysd-found-023.text: Some addresses are set once and never change; others are lent for a while. A static IP address is configured persistently, so network infrastructure such as routers and mail servers typically uses static addressing. Static addresses are usually more expensive but more reliable, and they suit remote access and server hosting. A dynamic address is assigned by the network each time a host joins or restarts, most often with {{ref:sysd-found-146}}. That spares administrators from assigning an address to each device. A DHCP address carries a lease, and an unrenewed lease may be given to another device.

sysd-found-146.title: DHCP: how a device gets its address automatically
sysd-found-146.text: A device joining a network needs an address, and nobody has to type one in. The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices on a network. A central DHCP server manages a pool of addresses and parameters such as the default gateway and name servers. DHCP is connectionless and runs over UDP. The server listens on port 67 and the client on port 68, and a joining client sends a broadcast query for its configuration. A server can allocate addresses three ways. A dynamic address is leased from a reserved range and reclaimed if unrenewed. An automatic one is permanent. A manual one is mapped by an administrator from a client ID or MAC address. A broadcast stays on its own subnet, so relay agents on routers forward it by unicast to configured DHCP servers. Base DHCP has no way to check who is sending a message. A rogue server can hand clients false information such as a DNS server, and a client can exhaust the address pool with fresh identifiers.

sysd-found-147.title: The DHCP handshake: discover, offer, request, acknowledge
sysd-found-147.text: Getting an address from DHCP takes four exchanges: discovery, offer, request and acknowledgement. The client starts with a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast to 255.255.255.255 or the subnet broadcast address. It may ask for a particular address that the server can take into account. A server that receives it reserves an address and replies with DHCPOFFER. That message carries the offered IP address, subnet mask, lease duration and the server's own address. The client may receive several offers but accepts only one. It broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST that names the chosen server, and the other servers withdraw their offers and return those addresses to their pools. The chosen server completes the exchange with a DHCPACK that carries the lease duration and any other configuration the client asked for. Before claiming an address, the client should probe it, for example with ARP, to see whether another host already uses it. The address is a lease. The client starts renewing once half the lease interval has passed, unicasting a DHCPREQUEST to the granting server. If that server stays unreachable, the client rebinds by broadcasting the request so any server can renew the lease. When a lease expires, the client must stop using the address and restart with a DHCPDISCOVER. Its address then changes, so ongoing connections break. A client may send DHCP Release to give up its address, but the protocol does not require it, because devices are often unplugged without warning.

sysd-found-027.title: Subnets and CIDR: where the network part ends
sysd-found-027.text: An IP address is really two addresses in one. The high-order bits are the network prefix, and the remaining bits, the host identifier, number the hosts within that network. A subnet is a part of an IP network, made by designating network prefixes within the address space. The subnet mask or CIDR notation determines where the split falls. In CIDR notation the address is followed by a slash and the number of bits of the network part. So 192.0.2.1 with mask 255.255.255.0 is written 192.0.2.1/24, because the first 24 bits indicate the network. Only IPv4 uses the term subnet mask, but both versions use CIDR.

sysd-found-162.title: The retransmission timeout: how long TCP waits before resending
sysd-found-162.text: How long should a TCP sender wait for an acknowledgment before resending? Networks vary so much that no fixed answer works, so the retransmission timeout (RTO) must be determined dynamically. It is computed by the algorithm in RFC 6298, which includes Karn's algorithm for taking samples of the {{ref:sysd-found-194}}. Successive timeouts for the same segment back off exponentially. The backed-off value is kept until a segment with new data has been sent and acknowledged without retransmission. An endpoint must implement slow start, congestion avoidance and {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}} of the RTO to avoid congestion collapse. Excessive retransmission of one segment signals a failed remote host or path. At a threshold called R1, which should be at least 3 retransmissions, TCP advises IP to start dead-gateway diagnosis. At a larger threshold, R2, which should be at least 100 seconds, it closes the connection. An application must be able to set R2 per connection. Opening a connection can fail the same way, through excessive SYN retransmissions, and R2 for a SYN must allow at least 3 minutes.

sysd-found-161.title: TCP segments and the maximum segment size
sysd-found-161.text: A program that makes one send call may see its data travel in several segments. TCP guarantees no correlation between the boundaries of segments and those of the application's read or write buffers. Segmentation is how TCP cuts the byte stream into segments, and the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option tells the peer the largest segment it will accept. Larger segments mean fewer packets in flight, fewer interrupts and layer crossings, and less header overhead, though the benefit shrinks as segments grow. Smaller segments avoid a datagram larger than the smallest MTU on the path, which means loss or fragmentation. Some firewalls and middleboxes drop fragmented packets or the ICMP messages about them. Without an MSS option the default send MSS is 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6. The effective send MSS is the smaller of two sizes. One is the peer's advertised MSS, which reflects its reassembly buffer. The other is the largest size the IP layer permits, less the TCP header and any IP options.

sysd-found-014.title: Nagle's algorithm: waiting to fill a packet
sysd-found-014.text: Waiting 200 ms is a long time when a keystroke must appear on screen. Nagle's algorithm makes TCP wait for a full packet of data before sending, grouping small messages into a single packet. By default TCP waits 200 ms for a full packet. That creates small but potentially serious delays when repeated constantly during a file transfer. In Telnet each keystroke is echoed back by the server before the user sees it, so the wait would be very annoying. Applications can set the TCP_NODELAY socket option to override the 200 ms delay and force output after writing a character or a line.

sysd-found-156.title: TCP sequence numbers: numbering every byte
sysd-found-156.text: At 100 Gbps, TCP can use up its entire sequence number space in around a third of a second. At 2 megabits per second the same job takes 4.5 hours. TCP gives every octet of data on a connection a sequence number, so the receiver can acknowledge, order and de-duplicate what it gets. Acknowledgments are cumulative: an acknowledgment of X means all octets up to but not including X have arrived. The sequence space is finite, from 0 to 2^32 - 1, so all sequence number arithmetic is done modulo 2^32. A new connection takes a 32-bit initial sequence number from a clock that typically ticks about every 4 microseconds and cycles in roughly 4.55 hours. Implementations should add a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key, because an attacker who could compute the number could guess sequence numbers. At high data rates the sequence space can wrap within the segment lifetime. TCP Timestamp Options and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) then detect and discard old duplicates.

sysd-found-008.title: Selective acknowledgment: resend only what is missing
sysd-found-008.text: Say the second of ten equal segments, covering sequence numbers 2,000 to 2,999, is lost. With only cumulative acknowledgments, the receiver can acknowledge nothing past 2,000, so the sender may have to resend everything from there. Selective acknowledgment (SACK) is a TCP option that lets the receiver acknowledge discontinuous blocks of correctly received data. The receiver sends a cumulative ACK of 2,000 plus a SACK option with sequence numbers 3,000 and 11,000, and the sender retransmits only the second segment. All popular TCP stacks support it, though it works only if both parties do. SACK can name a maximum of three blocks.

sysd-found-155.title: Why TCP needs three messages to open a connection
sysd-found-155.text: Why three messages and not two? The principal reason is to prevent old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion. The three-way handshake is the procedure TCP uses to establish a connection, in which the two peers exchange and acknowledge each other's initial sequence numbers. Each side sends a SYN carrying its own initial sequence number and needs it acknowledged. The acknowledgment of the first SYN and the second side's own SYN travel in one segment, which makes three messages. The handshake is needed because sequence numbers are not tied to a global clock. The receiver of a first SYN cannot know whether it is an old one, so it asks the sender to verify it. In the basic exchange the first SYN uses sequence number 100, so the reply acknowledges 101. A bare ACK takes no sequence space, because otherwise acknowledgments would themselves need acknowledging. Now suppose an old duplicate SYN reaches the passive peer. It replies normally, and the first peer sees the wrong acknowledgment and sends a RST. The passive peer returns to LISTEN, and the genuine SYN then completes the handshake. The procedure also works when both peers open at once, and an implementation must support this simultaneous open. Handshake segments may carry data, but the receiver must buffer it until the connection reaches ESTABLISHED.

sysd-found-157.title: The states a TCP connection moves through
sysd-found-157.text: A TCP connection moves through a fixed set of states during its life. They are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and the fictional CLOSED, which means no connection record exists. Incoming segments carrying SYN, ACK, RST or FIN, user calls and timeouts cause the changes. A passive OPEN means the process wants to accept incoming connection requests, and an active OPEN attempts to initiate one. Opening starts in LISTEN, which waits for a request from any remote peer. SYN-SENT has sent a request and awaits a matching one. SYN-RECEIVED has both received and sent one and awaits the acknowledgment. ESTABLISHED is the normal state for data transfer. Closing uses the other states. The FIN-WAIT states wait for the peer's termination request, and CLOSE-WAIT waits for the local user to close. CLOSING and LAST-ACK wait for acknowledgment of a termination request already sent. TIME-WAIT keeps delayed segments from earlier connections from affecting new ones.

sysd-found-013.title: SYN floods and TCP hijacking
sysd-found-013.text: A flood of bogus connection requests can swamp a server. In a SYN flood, an attacker uses a spoofed IP address and repeatedly sends crafted SYN packets. The server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections. SYN cookies and cryptographic puzzles have been proposed as defenses, though SYN cookies come with their own vulnerabilities. A connection can also be hijacked. An attacker who can eavesdrop on a session and redirect packets can learn the sequence number. The attacker then forges a segment that looks like the next one in the stream. That is why the initial sequence number should be unpredictable.
